South Pole, Gaïago Issue Europe’s First Gold Standard Soil Carbon Credits
- South Pole and Gaïago have issued the first carbon credits globally under Gold Standard’s Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, covering an initial 6,000 hectares in France and Belgium.
- Full enrollment across 727 farms will expand the European Soil Revitalization Programme to more than 39,000 hectares, with 264,174 tCO₂e of removals forecast during its first crediting period.
- The credits give corporate buyers a new European source of verified land-based removals as companies prepare for evolving SBTi requirements around ongoing and residual emissions.
South Pole, Gaïago and Gold Standard have issued the first carbon credits from a European regenerative agriculture programme covering farms in France and Belgium.
The issuance comes from the European Soil Revitalization Programme and covers its first 6,000 verified hectares. It is the first project globally to be design-certified and issue credits under Gold Standard’s Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology.
For corporate carbon buyers, the development opens a new source of verified removals in a sector where measurement and durability have often complicated investment.
Scaling soil carbon across European farms
The programme launched in 2022 and has a 20-year operational horizon. It currently brings together 727 farms across France and Belgium.
Once fully enrolled, the initiative will cover more than 39,282 hectares. It is forecast to remove 264,174 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent during its first crediting period.
Gaïago implements and operates the programme on the ground. South Pole has served as its carbon asset development partner since 2022. Its role includes project development and the verification processes needed to secure Gold Standard certification.
Farmers receive tailored support to introduce regenerative agricultural practices. These include reduced or zero tillage, which limits soil disturbance, and expanded year-round cover cropping. The practices are intended to increase soil carbon while improving water retention, nutrient levels and resilience.
Participants must also apply Gaïago’s NUTRIGEO L biostimulant. The product is designed to restore microbial diversity and improve soil structure.
The programme uses the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s GSOC MRV protocol and aligns with the FAO RECSOIL Initiative. So far, 1,972 local stakeholders have received training on soil health.
Carbon finance meets agricultural transition risk
Agricultural soils offer significant potential for carbon sequestration, but shifting farming practices can expose producers to financial and operational risks.
Carbon finance can help absorb some of those costs. For buyers, however, soil projects must demonstrate that claimed removals can be reliably measured and independently verified.
Aaron Barasz, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operations Officer at South Pole, said: “Trust and integrity are non-negotiable for carbon credit buyers. This milestone proves that soil carbon removals can be measured, verified, and delivered at scale under the highest international standards. Drawing on over 20 years of carbon asset expertise, South Pole is proud to help corporate buyers invest with confidence in high-impact, future-proof, diversified removal strategies.”
Vanessa Pezet, Gaïago Carbon Program Director, said: “Transitioning to regenerative agriculture requires financial backing and practical support for farmers on the frontlines of climate change. As project proponent, Gaïago is showing that restoring soil health directly reinforces farmer resilience and productivity. This issuance validates the dedication of hundreds of French and Belgian farmers leading the agroecological transition.”
RELATED ARTICLE: South Pole Welcomes Sustainability Veteran Dr. Daniel Klier as New CEO
New option for corporate carbon buyers
The issuance arrives as corporate carbon strategies face tighter scrutiny over credit quality and the appropriate role of removals.
SBTi’s evolving Corporate Net-Zero Standard is particularly relevant. Its proposed approach gives carbon credits a defined role in addressing emissions as companies progress toward net zero, increasing attention on credible removal supply.
Sarah Leugers, Chief Growth Officer at Gold Standard, said: “Without healthy soil, life on our planet cannot thrive. It is not only a critical tool to mitigate emissions through carbon sequestration but also supports sustainable agriculture and global food security. As the first project worldwide to issue credits under our Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, the European Soil Revitalization Programme shows how rigorous standards can unlock vital finance for sustainable land management. We congratulate Gaïago and South Pole on this important milestone.”
For investors and corporate buyers, the programme combines carbon removal with agricultural resilience and soil restoration. Its larger test will now be scale. If the model expands across its planned acreage while maintaining rigorous verification, it could strengthen Europe’s supply of land-based removals and channel more private climate finance directly into farming.

articles.title: South Korea's ESG disclosure framework: A welcome mandate, but lacking urgency - Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)
articles.summary: South Korea's ESG disclosure framework: A welcome mandate, but lacking urgency  Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)

source_detail.name: Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)

articles.full_text:
South Korea’s proposed mandatory environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure framework provides a phased mandate beginning in the financial year (FY) 2027 for firms with consolidated assets exceeding KRW10 trillion (USD7.41 billion), with the threshold falling to KRW5 trillion in FY2028 and potentially KRW2 trillion in FY2029.
Current voluntary reporting in South Korea highlights gaps in reliability and comprehensiveness. In 2025, while 68% of reporting firms disclosed Scope 3 emissions, only 49% explained their calculation methodologies, and just 13% disclosed reporting boundaries or underlying assumptions. Consolidated Scope 1 and 2 reporting also remained limited.
South Korea’s three-year safe harbor provision is broader than Japan’s, shielding nearly all disclosed information, including historical data, from liability. Assurance requirements also begin a year later, suggesting a more cautious approach to sustainability reporting.
South Korea’s disclosure framework should be paired with measures to support sustainable finance. A robust measurement system, sector-specific Scope 3 guidelines, and an expanded Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) database can support high-quality disclosure, while incentives and a mandatory green taxonomy could facilitate financing for sustainable activities.
South Korea's Financial Services Commission (FSC) released its proposed framework for mandatory environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosures in July 2026, following prolonged consultation with industry, the financial sector, and other stakeholders. The framework establishes standard guidelines for disclosing sustainability-related financial risks and opportunities. It is modeled on the International Financial Reporting Standards General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information (IFRS S1).
While the framework is a step in the right direction, it could do more to encourage sustainable finance. Designed as a standalone disclosure measure, it offers no new incentives to accelerate sustainable finance and leaves the existing, voluntary South Korean taxonomy (K-taxonomy) unchanged.
Gaps in the new ESG disclosure framework continue to constrain sustainable finance. The K-taxonomy remains voluntary, and there is a lack of stringent technical screening criteria for eligible activities. Additionally, clear guidelines on which activities can count toward the national climate finance investment target or the Korea Green Transformation (K-GX) plan are still needed. As long as activities with ambiguous sustainability benefits are included under the plan, investors in green-labeled instruments may question the credibility of K-GX issuances.
As the ESG disclosure framework has not yet been enacted into law, with amendments to the Capital Markets Act currently before the National Assembly, lawmakers still have an opportunity to strengthen it.
This commentary examines three aspects of the South Korean framework: the phased scope and timing, how its safe harbor and assurance provisions compare with Japan’s, and what is still needed to strengthen sustainable finance.
South Korea takes a phased approach to mandatory disclosure
South Korea’s ESG disclosure framework stands out in the region by establishing a firm, phased statutory disclosure mandate rather than relying on voluntary alignment. Companies must include sustainability disclosures in their business reports from the financial year (FY) 2027, beginning with Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI)-listed firms with consolidated assets exceeding KRW10 trillion (USD7.41 billion). The threshold falls to KRW5 trillion (USD3.70 billion) in FY2028 and potentially to KRW2 trillion (USD1.48 billion) in FY2029.
This approach is closer to the European Union’s (EU) Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) than to many Asian frameworks. Both the South Korean framework and the CSRD embed disclosure in statutory corporate filings rather than exchange listing rules; phase in coverage by company size rather than requiring universal compliance from day one; and build toward mandatory third-party assurance instead of allowing voluntary verification. Mandatory climate disclosure will be established in the Korea Sustainability Standards Board (KSSB) framework, which is expected to align with the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB).
Mandatory disclosure will institutionalize corporate ESG and climate reporting. Companies will have to measure their climate impacts and assess how these could affect their business. This is a significant shift from the current voluntary system. According to a Korea Exchange (KRX) analysis of 2025 disclosure data, a record 225 companies published voluntary sustainability reports, a 10% increase from the previous year. Among the largest domestic issuers — those with market capitalizations exceeding KRW10 trillion (USD7.41 billion) — 86% (50 of 58 firms) were already reporting voluntarily.
However, voluntary reporting has not produced reliable, complete data. Of the 225 companies that published sustainability reports, only three disclosed Scope 1 and 2 emissions on a consolidated basis, including emissions from subsidiaries. Standalone Scope 1 and 2 coverage, meanwhile, was reported by nearly all companies (99%). Value-chain disclosures also lack methodological consistency. While 68% of reporting firms disclosed Scope 3 emissions, only 49% explained their calculation methodologies, and just 13% disclosed specific reporting boundaries or underlying assumptions.
Between 2021 and 2025, the number of reporting companies nearly tripled, but Scope 3 coverage rose only from 66% to 68%. Reporting of Scope 1 and 2 emissions on a consolidated basis remained limited, with only seven companies providing this data in 2024 and just three in 2025. This underscores the limitations of voluntary standards, which do not independently ensure audit-ready, consolidated emissions data.
In a March 2026 opinion letter to the FSC, the National Pension Service (NPS) called for an earlier and broader mandate. It proposed that mandatory reporting begin in FY2026 and apply to companies with assets of KRW2 trillion (USD1.48 billion), arguing that South Korea's timeline lagged behind Singapore and Japan by two to three years. The final framework adopts a lower threshold in later phases, while retaining the KRW10 trillion threshold for the first cohort and a later start date.
How South Korea’s safe harbor and assurance provisions compare with Japan’s
The Sustainability Standards Board of Japan (SSBJ) framework, cited by the NPS as a similar regional example, offers a useful comparison on two features: assurance and safe harbor provisions. Together, these aspects determine how quickly disclosed data becomes trustworthy. Assurance is independent, third-party verification that disclosed data is accurate and complete, similar to a financial audit, but for sustainability information. Safe harbor provisions limit companies' liability for specified disclosures, typically forward-looking statements or information that cannot be readily verified, while reporting practices and data systems mature.
South Korea's new ESG disclosure framework provides a generous three-year liability exemption covering forward-looking, estimated, and third-party-sourced emissions data, as well as historical emissions data disclosed during the initial window. While some legal protection may be justified for new disclosure types, the extent and duration of the provision give companies a relatively long period to strengthen their reporting processes. In contrast, Japan's safe harbor provision is narrower. It covers only Scope 3 emissions and other forward-looking estimates, subject to methodology and reasoning documentation.
Japan also requires assurance sooner: one year after mandatory disclosure begins, compared with two years in South Korea. Japan’s first cohort, companies with market capitalizations exceeding JPY3 trillion (USD19.2 billion), must begin reporting for the financial year ending March 2027 and obtain assurance from the following year. In South Korea, assurance applies from FY2029, with the first assured disclosures published in 2030.
This comparison demonstrates that South Korea has moved more cautiously than Japan in designing these standards. It shields a wider range of disclosed information for longer, while requiring independent verification a year later. As a result, investors and regulators must rely on largely unverified data for longer, just when the new framework is being established.
Using disclosure to support sustainable finance
The South Korean ESG disclosure framework should be paired with a robust measurement system capable of supporting high-quality disclosure. While Scope 3 disclosure has been deferred until FY2030, with exemptions for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in non-high-carbon sectors, sector-specific Scope 3 calculation guidelines are being developed for 15 export sectors. A 1,000-entry Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) database aligned with the Global Life Cycle Assessment Data Access network (GLAD) system is also being developed. These initiatives are important steps toward building the infrastructure needed to measure and track corporate emissions.
Consistent and comparable reporting can also provide a foundation for broader sustainable finance activity. The FSC could build on the disclosure regime by introducing incentives for sustainable finance and refining the K-taxonomy to facilitate funding for sustainable activities. These measures could, in turn, strengthen the credibility of issuances under the K-GX plan.
The ESG disclosure framework places a welcome emphasis on measurement, data infrastructure, and reporting systems. More comprehensive information can help companies identify and manage climate-related risks, improve their emissions performance, and advance their decarbonization and sustainability goals.

South Korea Announces $747 Billion Energy Transition Plan Through 2035
- South Korea’s K-GX strategy mobilizes $747 billion through 2035, combining government spending and climate finance to accelerate the country’s energy transition.
- The government targets 100 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030 and wants electric and hydrogen vehicles to exceed 70% of new vehicle sales by 2035.
- Five high-emitting sectors, including steel, cement and semiconductors, will face targeted decarbonization plans as Seoul responds to tighter global carbon rules.
South Korea has unveiled a $747 billion energy transition and decarbonization strategy through 2035, putting industrial transformation at the center of its climate and economic agenda.
The K-GX, or Korea-Green Transformation, plan combines roughly $149 billion in fiscal spending with more than $590 billion in climate finance. The government also expects about $164 billion in separate private-sector investment.
Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il presented the strategy alongside senior government officials and business leaders.
President Lee Jae Myung said South Korea should use its technological and manufacturing capabilities to compete for leadership in the emerging green economy. “We must move away from the practice of chasing others and become architects and leaders of the green market ourselves,” Lee said.
Renewable power and transport take priority
The government is targeting 100 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. It also plans support for green steel, batteries, solar power, wind energy, hydrogen and small modular reactors.
Transport is another major pillar.
Electric and hydrogen-powered vehicles are expected to account for more than 70% of new vehicle sales by 2035. That target would require a significant shift across South Korea’s automotive industry and supporting infrastructure.
The strategy also seeks to strengthen domestic supply chains for critical clean-energy technologies.
South Korea plans to commercialize tandem solar cells by 2028. Support will also extend to advanced batteries, power semiconductors, carbon capture technologies and small modular reactors.
Heavy industry faces faster decarbonization
K-GX targets five of South Korea’s highest-emitting industrial sectors: steel, petrochemicals, refining, cement, and semiconductors and displays.
These industries sit at the intersection of the country’s export economy and its climate obligations. Decarbonizing them will require substantial capital expenditure, new technologies and greater access to low-carbon energy.
The government plans to develop sector-specific decarbonization roadmaps to support its 2035 emissions targets.
Steel is a particular focus. South Korea wants to become the first country to mass-produce hydrogen-reduced steel and use that capability to compete in the global green steel market.
The strategy also covers 10 green industries that Seoul sees as potential engines of future growth. These include electric vehicles, power semiconductors and carbon capture technologies.
RELATED ARTICLE: AI Power Surge Pushes South Korea Toward Nuclear
Climate finance tied to emissions impact
The scale of K-GX reflects an effort to reduce the financial risk attached to technologies that may require years of development before reaching commercial scale.
Projects receiving climate-finance support will be assessed according to their greenhouse gas reduction impact. That approach links public and financial-sector capital more directly to measurable decarbonization outcomes.
Climate Ministry officials said the strategy responds to rising physical climate risks, energy security concerns and increasingly stringent carbon regulation in international markets.
For South Korea’s export-heavy economy, those pressures are becoming increasingly difficult to separate from industrial policy. Carbon requirements can affect production costs, supply chains and market access, particularly for emissions-intensive manufacturers.
The government is therefore positioning carbon neutrality not only as an environmental obligation, but also as a source of future economic growth.
Government seeks to share transition risk
Private investment will be critical to delivering the strategy.
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, who heads the private-sector consultative body supporting K-GX, said the plan showed the government’s willingness to share investment risks with businesses.
Companies have been hesitant to commit to long-term carbon-neutrality projects amid uncertainty over technologies, markets and policy.
K-GX attempts to address that constraint by combining public expenditure, climate finance and private capital on a scale designed to move projects from development into commercial deployment.
For investors and corporate leaders, implementation will now be the key test. Capital allocation, emissions measurement and sector roadmaps will determine how effectively the headline funding translates into lower emissions.
South Korea’s approach also reflects a wider shift in climate policy. Governments are increasingly linking decarbonization with industrial competitiveness, energy security and domestic manufacturing.
For one of Asia’s largest industrial economies, the next decade will test whether that combination can turn climate spending into both emissions reductions and durable economic advantage.

articles.title: Case Study: Apollo implements new EUDR compliance technology - European Rubber Journal
articles.summary: Case Study: Apollo implements new EUDR compliance technology  European Rubber Journal
articles.full_text:
"Implementation strengthens our ability to establish end-to-end visibility from source to finished product” 
Gurugram, India – Apollo Tyres has partnered with Emertech Innovations to establish an integrated compliance and traceability system for its natural rubber (NR) supply-chain under the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
The implementation covers 56,491 source plots spanning around 150,000 hectares across India and several international sourcing markets, according to an Emertech case-study published 5 Oct.
The plot data, said the technology partner, comprises 43,932 point-based plots and 12,559 polygon-based plots within Apollo's NR supplier network.
The process involves five stages – engage; validate; assess; trace and file – each building on the one before, with an administrative portal that gives Apollo’s teams one view across all of them.
Under the system, NR suppliers submit GeoJSON files, sourcing information, risk evidence and supporting documents through a dedicated supplier portal.
The platform checks submissions for file structure, coordinates, geometry and mandatory plot information, as well as the correct use of points or polygons.
Using a satellite-based deforestation analysis tool, Emertech examines land within the submitted plot boundaries, comparing historical satellite imagery with current forest-cover and land-use information.
The analysis, it said, assesses evidence of changes after the EUDR regulatory cut-off date of 31 Dec 2020 and assigns a risk result to each plot.
The system also flags potentially risky plots which will be “held for review” before being allowed into the compliant supply-chain.
Emertech has “integrated” the compliance platform with Apollo's existing ERP and operational systems, allowing validated supplier and plot information to be linked to all supply-chain documents.
These include purchase-orders, incoming consignment notes, goods receipts, material and batch records, production transactions, finished products and export shipments.
As described by Emertech, the process maintains the connection “from the land where the NR originated to the product eventually placed on the European market.”
For EU-bound shipments, the system consolidates the applicable source-plot information and prepares the relevant due diligence statement.
Furthermore, the platform is integrated with the EU Information System within the TRACES NT environment, allowing statements to be filed directly with the EU system.
Submission status and reference numbers are subsequently returned to Apollo's central “administrative portal,” which provides “one view across every stage for compliance, procurement and operational teams.”
The portal also maintains a record linking all declarations with the suppliers, source plots, risk evidence, production records and shipment concerned.
“EUDR requires a high degree of transparency and traceability across the NR supply chain,” said Shibu George, group head, advanced manufacturing & enterprise application, at Apollo Tyres.
The collaboration with Emertech, he added, had enabled Apollo to bring together “sourcing, traceability and geospatial validation capabilities at scale,” covering a significant NR sourcing footprint.
“This implementation strengthens our ability to establish end-to-end visibility from source to finished product,” concluded George.

articles.summary: Circular Economy  The Statesman
articles.full_text:
In a statement, the Ministry of Defence stated that under this campaign, the disposal of unserviceable items and e-waste kept in the premises of the ministry was done in two phases.
For decades, India has treated waste as the end of the production cycle. But as the country urbanises, electrifies and digitises, discarded batteries, vehicles, electronics, tyres, plastics and metals are becoming something else: a vast, underused pool of industrial resources. The circular economy is built on a simple proposition ~ materials should remain in productive use for as long as possible, and what is discarded should become an input for what comes next. The opportunity is substantial.
The Economic Survey 2024-25 cited an estimate that greater resource circularity could generate cost savings equivalent to 11 per cent of current GDP by 2030 and 30 per cent by 2050. These are projections, not guaranteed gains, but they illustrate why circularity deserves to be considered an industrial policy issue rather than simply an environmental one. India’s resource challenge is becoming more acute precisely as its industrial ambitions expand. It wants more electronics, vehicles, renewable-energy equipment, batteries, buildings and infrastructure.
Advertisement
Every one of these sectors consumes materials. The question is whether the country’s future demand will be met predominantly by extracting and importing more virgin resources, or increasingly by recovering materials already embedded in the domestic economy. The numbers from India’s waste streams are beginning to make the case. A NITI Aayog assessment from early this year projects e-waste generation to rise from 6.19 million tonnes in 2024 to 14 million tonnes by 2030. The same assessment projects lithium-ion battery demand to rise from 29 GWh in 2025 to 248 GWh by 2035.
Advertisement
End-of-life vehicles are projected to increase from 23 million in 2025 to 50 million by 2030. These are not separate environmental problems, but emerging industrial resource pools. Consider critical minerals. India imports many of the materials needed for advanced electronics, electric mobility and clean-energy technologies. Recycling cannot eliminate this dependence: NITI Aayog itself cautions that recycling will only partially satisfy demand for several battery minerals. But it can create a secondary source of supply, particularly for materials such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and other strategically important elements. This explains an important policy development in 2025.
The Union government approved a Rs 1,500-crore incentive scheme for critical-mineral recycling under the National Critical Mineral Mission. Eligible feedstock includes e-waste, spent lithium-ion batteries and scrap such as catalytic converters from end-of-life vehicles. The significance is larger than the size of the subsidy: recycling is being recognised as part of resource security.
India has also built a regulatory architecture around Extended Producer Responsibility, under which producers are assigned responsibility for managing products after their useful life. The framework now covers plastic packaging, batteries, e-waste, tyres, used oil, end-of-life vehicles and other material streams. In 2025, the government also introduced frameworks for end-of-life vehicles, construction and demolition waste and non-ferrous scrap. There is evidence that this architecture is beginning to create a formal recycling market.
As of mid 2026, government data recorded 2,986 registered plastic-waste recyclers, 520 battery-waste recyclers, 579 tyre-waste recyclers and 386 e-waste recyclers. The reported quantities recycled were 19.697 million tonnes of plastic waste, 6.937 million tonnes of battery waste, 12.229 million tonnes of tyre waste and 2.875 million tonnes of e-waste. Yet these numbers should not encourage complacency. Recycling capacity on paper is not the same thing as a functioning circular economy. India’s central difficulty is collection, traceability and economics.
Valuable materials often fail to reach formal recyclers. Informal networks remain deeply embedded in collection and dismantling. NITI Aayog’s January 2026 assessment notes that rapidly growing e-waste and lithium-ion battery waste are still substantially managed through informal channels, often using unsafe processing methods. It recommends stronger auditing, common recycling facilities, better collection systems and the formalisation of informal workers rather than simply attempting to eliminate them. This is where policy must become more sophisticated.
A circular economy cannot be built merely by announcing recycling targets. Someone must collect the discarded product, transport it economically, identify its composition, dismantle it safely and recover materials at a purity that industry is willing to buy. If virgin material remains cheaper than recovered material, regulation alone will struggle to create a durable market. The same problem applies to small businesses. India’s recycling ecosystem will not be transformed entirely by large corporations. Thousands of micro and small enterprises already operate close to waste streams and manufacturing clusters. The government’s MSE-SPICE scheme, with an outlay of Rs 472.5 crore for 2023-24 to 2026-27, provides capital subsidy support for eligible circular-economy projects.
Its sectors include plastics, rubber, electronic waste, lithium-ion batteries, end-of-life vehicles, scrap metals and solar panels. But implementation remains the harder test. Under MSE-SPICE, the government has approved a technology deck covering 116 circular-economy technologies, yet the latest MSME Annual Report 2025–26 records only 10 MSEs receiving capital-subsidy support so far. The contrast between the scale of the policy ambition and its limited adoption points to a wider challenge: India’s circular-economy transition will depend not merely on announcing incentives, but on making technology, finance and compliance accessible enough for smaller firms to participate.
The next phase therefore requires a shift from waste management to material management. India needs reliable material-flow data, stronger standards for recycled inputs, better testing and certification, cheaper financing for recycling plants and predictable demand from manufacturers. Government procurement could help create markets for certified recycled materials. Product design should consider repairability, durability and eventual recovery. The renewable-energy transition makes this particularly urgent.
Solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles and electronic equipment are being deployed precisely because India wants a cleaner and more technologically sophisticated economy. But the transition cannot simply move environmental costs downstream. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has already launched an innovation challenge focused on circularity in batteries and solar photovoltaic technologies, including recycling, reuse and resource efficiency. India therefore faces a choice about what kind of industrial power it wants to become.
It can remain predominantly a large consumer of imported primary resources while treating discarded materials as a municipal burden. Or it can build an industry that mines the urban economy for metals, components and materials already paid for once. The second model will not replace conventional mining, manufacturing or imports. Nor will recycling by itself solve India’s environmental problems. Its significance lies elsewhere: it can make Indian industry more resource-efficient, create new manufacturing and technology markets, improve supply-chain resilience and reduce the quantity of economic value lost when products become waste. The industrial opportunity in circularity is not found at the garbage dump. It lies in redesigning the relationship between production and disposal. For a country seeking to become a major manufacturing economy while securing critical resources, that relationship may prove to be one of the most consequential industrial policy questions of the next decade.
(The writer is an author, policy analyst, and columnist, currently serving as The Statement Fellow and Coordinator, South Asia at Students For Liberty)

articles.summary:
Isometric has certified a new carbon removal methodology for grazing lands, creating a framework for projects that increase soil carbon while supporting ranching livelihoods and land restoration. The Grazing Lands […]
The post Isometric Certifies Soil Carbon Module for 260 Million Hectares of U.S. Grazing Land appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Isometric Certifies Soil Carbon Module for 260 Million Hectares of U.S. Grazing Land
- Isometric has certified a new Grazing Lands Management Module covering soil carbon removal through rotational grazing, improved forage, water management and brush management.
- Projects must demonstrate measurable soil carbon gains, meet additionality requirements and account for methane, imported feed and changes in agricultural productivity.
- Grassroots Carbon and Cultivo are the first developers to adopt the framework, bringing more than 2 million hectares of managed and contracted U.S. land into their respective portfolios.
Isometric has certified a new carbon removal methodology for grazing lands, creating a framework for projects that increase soil carbon while supporting ranching livelihoods and land restoration.
The Grazing Lands Management Module covers practices including rotational grazing, improved forage species, water management and brush management. It is the second supporting module under Isometric’s Improved Soil Management Protocol. A Cropland Management Module was certified in July 2026.
The certification followed a 30-day public consultation involving carbon buyers, suppliers and academics. It comes as carbon markets seek stronger measurement and additionality requirements for nature-based removals.
Soils hold nearly 3 trillion tonnes of carbon globally. Changes in land management can increase those stocks as plants capture atmospheric carbon dioxide and transfer carbon below ground through roots and decomposition.
A flexible approach with strict measurement
Rather than prescribing a single land management practice, the module allows developers to select interventions suited to individual properties.
These can include moving livestock between pastures to allow vegetation to recover. Projects may also introduce deep-rooted grasses and legumes, improve irrigation or install watering points that distribute livestock more evenly.
Brush management is another eligible approach. Managed fire or machinery can be used to control woody vegetation and restore grassland health.
Flexibility on land management is paired with tighter requirements around carbon accounting.
Projects must demonstrate increases in soil carbon by repeatedly sampling fixed locations or using independently validated biogeochemical models. Modelled results must be checked against physical soil measurements at least every five years.
Developers must also show that the practices were neither already in place nor common practice. Projects are additionally required to pass the Improved Soil Management Protocol’s financial additionality test.
Changes in agricultural productivity must be assessed against regional benchmarks. This is designed to prevent broader conditions, such as drought, from distorting project results.
Additional emissions also count. Methane from livestock and emissions associated with imported feed must be incorporated when calculating net carbon removal.
Landowners guaranteed a share of revenue
The methodology also introduces social and environmental safeguards that extend beyond carbon accounting.
Projects must maintain meaningful community engagement throughout their lifetime. Enrolled landowners must receive at least 20% of project revenue, reflecting their role in maintaining soil carbon stocks.
Grassroots Carbon and Cultivo are the first developers planning to generate certificates under the module.
Grassroots Carbon works with more than 340 ranching families across 22 U.S. states. Its programs cover more than 1.2 million hectares and have paid ranchers $40 million for increasing soil carbon. The company expects cumulative payments to exceed $68 million by the end of 2026.
RELATED ARTICLE: Isometric Expands Carbon Removal Certification to China
“The more than 260 million hectares of U.S. grazing lands represent an extraordinary opportunity to deliver measurable carbon removal at scale while strengthening ranching livelihoods, improving water outcomes, and supporting biodiversity. Isometric’s Grazing Lands Management Module recognizes that every ranch is different while grounding carbon removal in rigorous soil measurement. We’re excited to partner with Isometric to turn buyer confidence into sustained investment that supports working lands and sustains the ranching families who steward them,” said Brad Tipper, CEO of Grassroots Carbon.
Carbon buyers push for measurable outcomes
Cultivo has more than 800,000 hectares of U.S. grasslands contracted. Its expansion is backed by a $100 million capital deployment from Octopus Energy Generation.
“Soil carbon only works at scale if buyers can trust the numbers. The Grazing Lands Management Module requires soil carbon gains to be demonstrated through direct sampling or validated models, and issues certificates on a conservative basis. That gives us a rigorous framework we can apply across our grassland portfolio,” said Dr. Manuel Piñuela, CEO and co-founder of Cultivo.
Isometric developed the module through its in-house Science Team and reviewers from its independent Science Network, which includes more than 500 academic experts.
For carbon buyers and investors, the framework addresses a central challenge facing soil carbon markets: proving that claimed removals are measurable, additional and durable enough to justify investment.
Its broader importance will depend on whether rigorous measurement can operate economically across millions of hectares. If it can, U.S. grazing land could become a larger source of verified carbon removals while directing carbon finance toward the landowners responsible for maintaining those gains.

articles.title: Nestlé, Unilever, L&G Among 130 Firms Giving Governments 12 Months to Redirect $2.6 Trillion in Nature-Harming Subsidies
articles.summary:
A fiscal ask, with a clock on it More than 130 businesses and financial institutions published an open letter on 6 October calling on governments to overhaul the subsidies, tax […]
The post Nestlé, Unilever, L&G Among 130 Firms Giving Governments 12 Months to Redirect $2.6 Trillion in Nature-Harming Subsidies appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Nestlé, Unilever, L&G Among 130 Firms Giving Governments 12 Months to Redirect $2.6 Trillion in Nature-Harming Subsidies
- More than 130 companies and financial institutions, representing over $600 billion in revenue and $4.7 trillion in assets under management, want governments to start national incentive reform processes within 12 months.
- The letter targets at least $2.6 trillion a year in public spending that degrades soil, water and ecosystems, and frames the fix as redirecting existing money, not raising new funds.
- Only 5% of countries have set comprehensive national targets under the UN biodiversity framework’s subsidy commitment, which puts governments on the defensive at COP17 in Yerevan.
A fiscal ask, with a clock on it
More than 130 businesses and financial institutions published an open letter on 6 October calling on governments to overhaul the subsidies, tax breaks and other public incentives that reward the depletion of natural resources. Signatories include Nestlé, Unilever, Danone, H&M Group, Aldi Sued, Mahindra Group, Ørsted, Vattenfall, Legal & General, Rabobank, BNP Paribas Asset Management and Storebrand Asset Management.
The letter, convened by Business for Nature and the Finance for Biodiversity Foundation, lands two weeks before the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) opens in Yerevan, Armenia, on 19 October. It also precedes the G20 and the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings.
Its central request is procedural and time-bound. Governments are asked to set up cross-ministerial national processes within the next 12 months and to write incentive reform plans jointly with business, finance, producers, civil society, local communities and Indigenous Peoples.
The $2.6 trillion argument
The signatories put the scale of the problem at a minimum of $2.6 trillion a year in public spending, close to 2.5% of global GDP. Their case is that this spending distorts market signals, hides nature-related risk in asset prices and leaves companies that invest in resilient supply chains at a cost disadvantage against competitors that do not.
The pitch to finance ministries is that no new money is required. The letter argues the gain comes from changing what current budgets reward, and says existing national efforts show reform works when it is “carefully phased, designed with producers” and protective of livelihoods.
Corporate signatories tied the issue to operations. L’Occitane en Provence said about 90% of its raw materials contain at least one plant-derived ingredient. Danone pointed to the economic and environmental pressure on farmers, and Vattenfall to the multi-decade life of its assets and the need for predictable conditions.
Governments are behind on their own commitment
The demand is not new policy. Under Target 18 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, 196 countries agreed to identify harmful incentives by 2025 and cut them by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. According to Business for Nature, only 5% have set comprehensive national targets.
That gap is the letter’s leverage. COP17 is the point at which country progress against the framework is reviewed, and the first deadline has already passed. “Every year of delay pushes money in the wrong direction,” said Hans Stegeman, Chief Economist at Triodos Bank, who also called out continued public support for fossil fuels.
Anita de Horde, Co-Founding Executive Director of the Finance for Biodiversity Foundation, made the investor version of the point: financial institutions cannot be expected to align portfolios with nature while public incentives pull capital the other way.
RELATED ARTICLE: Nestlé, PepsiCo, Unilever Support Ellen MacArthur Foundation’s 2030 Plastics Agenda
What the signatory list shows
The coalition is weighted toward European consumer goods, food, retail and asset management, with a smaller group from Japan, Taiwan, India and Brazil. No US-headquartered company appears among the 44 names listed as major signatories; Federated Hermes Limited is the London-based arm of a US parent. Oil and gas majors, agricultural commodity traders and miners, the sectors most exposed to subsidy reform, are also absent from that tier.
The letter is also narrower than its predecessor. Business for Nature’s statement ahead of COP16 in 2024 drew 132 signatories with a reported $1.1 trillion in combined revenue and covered five broad policy areas. This year’s version carries a single ask and a larger financial sector presence, measured in assets under management.
Signatories commit to three things in return: assessing and disclosing nature dependencies and impacts, building resource security into strategy, and supplying governments with practical input on reform design. None of these is a new or binding pledge.
Private capital is not waiting, some argue
Market participants were quick to position existing mechanisms as part of the answer. “The tools needed to scale private investment into nature already exist,” said Emma Toovey, Chief Nature Officer at Environment Bank, citing England’s Biodiversity Net Gain regime. The company says it has committed £240 million to a national network of habitat banks. Compliance markets of that kind operate alongside subsidy reform and do not replace it.
What executives and investors should watch
- Yerevan outcomes on Target 18. Whether COP17 produces a reporting requirement or timeline for national incentive reform plans, or leaves the 2030 goal without interim checks.
- First movers. Which governments announce a cross-ministerial process within the 12-month window, and whether agriculture and finance ministries are both in the room.
- Sector exposure. Agriculture, food, energy and water-intensive industries face the most direct repricing if subsidies shift. Companies with disclosed nature dependencies will be better placed to model it.
- Signatory follow-through. Whether the commitments on disclosure translate into TNFD-aligned reporting and public positions on specific national subsidies.

articles.full_text:
Mars Petcare Appoints Vivian Ribeiro as Global Nature Manager
- Mars Petcare has appointed Vivian Ribeiro as Global Nature Manager, with a remit spanning deforestation, land-use monitoring and supply chain emissions.
- Ribeiro will support DCF and emissions strategies covering palm oil, pulp and paper, soy and beef, linking sourcing decisions to Mars’ wider climate targets.
- The appointment adds technical expertise in geospatial monitoring, EUDR risk assessment and supplier engagement as Mars strengthens oversight of forest-risk commodities.
Mars Petcare has appointed Vivian Ribeiro as Global Nature Manager, bringing a specialist in deforestation risk, land-use monitoring and sustainable sourcing into its global nature team.
Ribeiro joins from land-tech company Meridia, where she most recently served as VP of Methodology and R&D. At Meridia, Ribeiro worked on land-use and land-cover change mapping, supplier engagement and risk assessments linked to the EU Deforestation Regulation.
At Mars Petcare, Ribeiro will support the development of deforestation and conversion-free, or DCF, strategies alongside emissions work for palm oil, pulp and paper, soy and beef.
From land-use data to sourcing decisions
Ribeiro spent almost three years at Meridia, initially joining as an advisor in early 2024. During that period, she helped build the company’s consulting, methodology and R&D capabilities.
Her work covered land-use and land-cover change mapping, supplier engagement and risk assessments linked to the EU Deforestation Regulation. It also included methodologies for determining whether commodities were sourced without deforestation or conversion of other natural ecosystems.
Announcing the move, Ribeiro said: “After almost three years, I’ve left Meridia to join Mars Petcare as Global Nature Manager. I started at Meridia in early 2024 as an advisor and stayed to build the consulting, methodology, and R&D work. Most of it came down to understand how do you show, with evidence, that a product didnt cost a forest, a savanna or other natural lands.”
The move places that expertise inside a major downstream buyer. Mars Petcare operates across pet nutrition, veterinary health, diagnostics and technology, with 100,000 associates across more than 130 countries.
For its pet food business, agricultural commodities create direct exposure to land-use and supply chain risks. Mars has identified beef, cocoa, palm oil, pulp and paper, and soy as the five raw materials with the greatest deforestation impact across the wider group.
Mars strengthens oversight of forest-risk commodities
Mars says those five commodities account for more than half of its land-use area and more than 87% of greenhouse gas emissions linked to land-use change.
Its strategy combines supply chain mapping, supplier engagement and ongoing compliance monitoring. The company follows the Accountability Framework Initiative in implementing its DCF commitments.
The latest company data shows Mars reduced land use associated with its value chain by approximately 8.6% in 2025 compared with its 2015 baseline. It also reported a 16.9% reduction in value chain greenhouse gas emissions over the same period.
RELATED ARTICLE: Mars Reaches 98% Responsible Cocoa Sourcing
Mars is targeting a 50% reduction in value chain emissions by 2030 and net zero by 2050. Redesigning supply chains to stop deforestation is one of the core elements of that roadmap.
Ribeiro said her new position would connect technical monitoring with sourcing decisions further downstream. “At Mars I’ll support the development of the DCF and emissions strategy for palm, pulp and paper, soy and beef. That includes the methodologies and technical developments behind monitoring land use and land cover change.”
Why the appointment matters for corporate nature strategy
For C-suite sustainability and procurement teams, the appointment reflects a broader shift in nature governance. Corporate commitments increasingly require traceable evidence that sourcing decisions are not contributing to forest loss or ecosystem conversion.
That creates demand for stronger geospatial data, supplier-level verification and methodologies capable of translating satellite observations into procurement decisions.
Ribeiro highlighted the reach of those decisions across agricultural value chains. “Mars sits downstream, and from there a single sourcing decision travels back up the chain through a lot of hands, from suppliers all the way to the people working the land. That reach is what drew me to join. There’s a lot for me to learn here, and I’m excited to get started.”
For Mars Petcare, that downstream reach makes nature strategy a procurement and governance issue as much as an environmental one. The challenge now is converting better monitoring into sourcing decisions that reduce land conversion and emissions at scale.

articles.title: DOE Backs Vistra Nuclear Upgrades With $4.2 Billion Loan Commitment
articles.summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy is preparing to provide up to $4.2 billion in financing for upgrades to Vistra’s nuclear fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio. The investment targets existing reactors […]
The post DOE Backs Vistra Nuclear Upgrades With $4.2 Billion Loan Commitment appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
DOE Backs Vistra Nuclear Upgrades With $4.2 Billion Loan Commitment
- The U.S. Department of Energy has conditionally committed up to $4.2 billion to nuclear uprates and modernization across Vistra’s fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio.
- The projects are expected to preserve nearly 4 GW of existing nuclear generation and add 433 MW of new capacity across the PJM power market.
- Vistra plans to extend operations at three nuclear plants by another 20 years beyond their existing licenses, while supporting about 3,000 project-related jobs.
The U.S. Department of Energy is preparing to provide up to $4.2 billion in financing for upgrades to Vistra’s nuclear fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio. The investment targets existing reactors as electricity demand rises across one of America’s largest power markets.
The conditional loan commitment comes from the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing. It will support nuclear uprates and modernization at Vistra facilities serving the PJM Interconnection.
The projects could preserve nearly 4 GW of baseload generation, enough to power more than 3 million homes. They are also expected to add 433 MW of nuclear capacity without requiring equivalent new generation resources or transmission corridors.
“President Trump promised to unleash an American nuclear renaissance, and the Energy Department is delivering,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, around-the-clock energy for American families and businesses.”
Existing reactors become a capacity strategy
Vistra plans investments at the Beaver Valley nuclear plant in Pennsylvania and the Davis-Besse and Perry facilities in Ohio.
Rather than building reactors from scratch, the projects aim to extract additional electricity from existing nuclear assets. They would also support plant operations for an additional 20 years beyond their current licenses.
That approach is gaining relevance as utilities and policymakers confront rising power demand alongside lengthy timelines for new generation and transmission infrastructure.
The financing advances President Donald Trump’s Executive Order, Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base. The administration has positioned nuclear energy as a central part of its strategy for energy security, grid reliability and domestic industrial growth.
“President Trump and Secretary Wright have set a clear direction for America’s nuclear future, and EDF is financing the projects that advance that mission,” said EDF Director Gregory A. Beard. “These investments will extend the life of existing reactors, increase nuclear generation, and deliver abundant, around-the-clock power to lower costs and power American prosperity for decades to come.”
RELATED ARTICLE: U.S. Department of the Treasury, IRS Release Final Rules to Ensure Good-Paying Clean Energy Jobs, Expand Clean Energy Workforce
PJM demand puts firm power in focus
The investment has implications beyond the three plants.
PJM spans 13 states and faces growing pressure to secure enough generation as electricity consumption increases. Nuclear plants offer around-the-clock generation without the direct carbon emissions associated with fossil fuel power.
For companies with expanding electricity requirements, including data centers and advanced manufacturing facilities, maintaining existing nuclear capacity can also reduce exposure to power supply constraints.
DOE estimates the projects will support about 3,000 jobs tied to engineering, construction and planned outage work. Thousands of permanent positions associated with the plants would also be preserved.
The conditional commitment contains another potential expansion. DOE could finance future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant in Texas, extending the financing strategy beyond PJM.
Financing remains conditional
The $4.2 billion commitment is not yet a finalized loan.
Vistra must meet technical, legal, environmental and financial requirements before DOE enters definitive financing agreements or releases funding. That process leaves execution, regulatory and project risks in place.
For investors and corporate energy buyers, however, the proposed financing illustrates how U.S. energy policy is shifting toward maximizing existing nuclear infrastructure.
Extending reactor lives and increasing output can add firm generation faster than developing entirely new nuclear facilities. It can also preserve large volumes of carbon-free electricity already embedded in regional grids.
If completed as planned, the Pennsylvania and Ohio investments will keep almost 4 GW of nuclear generation operating while adding hundreds of megawatts of new capacity. Their broader importance lies in how the U.S. finances the next phase of power demand: not only through new projects, but by extracting more value from infrastructure already on the grid.

ABN AMRO Sustainable Impact Fund and Aviva Investors have committed approximately $112 million to SL Materials, backing the European expansion of technology that turns demolished concrete into raw material for […]

articles.full_text:
ABN AMRO, Aviva Investors Commit $112 Million to Scale Circular Concrete
- ABN AMRO Sustainable Impact Fund and Aviva Investors have committed approximately $112 million to circular concrete producer SL Materials.
- The capital will expand production in the Netherlands and support new sites across Europe, increasing access to recovered cementitious materials, sand and gravel.
- The investment targets a major construction decarbonisation challenge: reducing demand for virgin materials while cutting emissions associated with concrete production.
ABN AMRO Sustainable Impact Fund and Aviva Investors have committed approximately $112 million to SL Materials, backing the European expansion of technology that turns demolished concrete into raw material for new construction.
The follow on investment will finance additional production capacity, new European sites and further development of the company’s circular concrete technology.
Formerly known as Urban Mine, SL Materials is entering its next growth phase with a new name and larger capital base. Its expansion comes as Europe pushes the construction sector toward lower emissions and greater resource efficiency.
Turning demolition waste into new concrete
SL Materials has developed technology that recovers valuable components from concrete generated during demolition projects.
Its proprietary Smart Liberator and Smart Refiner technologies separate concrete into cementitious materials, sand and gravel. These materials can then return to the construction supply chain for use in new concrete.
The model addresses two environmental pressures at once. It reduces the volume of demolition material treated as waste and lowers reliance on virgin construction resources.
Concrete remains one of the world’s most widely used construction materials. Its production also carries a substantial carbon footprint, particularly from cement. Technologies that allow materials to remain in circulation for longer could therefore play a growing role in construction-sector decarbonisation.
For developers and contractors, circular concrete could also reduce exposure to raw material constraints as European resource-efficiency rules tighten.
$112 million backs European expansion
The new capital will expand SL Materials’ existing production facility in Zaandam, Netherlands. It will also support additional production capacity at new locations across Europe.
Part of the investment will fund continued innovation and optimisation of the company’s technology. The goal is to make recovered concrete materials available to a broader customer base at commercial scale.
The financing follows earlier backing from ABN AMRO through its Sustainable Impact Fund. For the bank, the follow-on commitment reflects a longer-term investment thesis around circularity and industrial decarbonisation.
RELATED ARTICLE: ABN AMRO Publishes Climate Strategy and Joins the Net Zero Banking Alliance
Maarten Blomme, Head of Corporate Investments at ABN AMRO, said: “We are convinced that circular concrete can become the industry standard. This follow-on investment will enable SL Materials to further scale its unique concrete recovery technology and make high-quality circular concrete available to a wider customer base. Financing innovative companies such as SL Materials is an important part of how ABN AMRO supports the transition to a more circular and resilient economy, and we are proud to support that ambition.”
The financing also coincides with the company’s transition from Urban Mine to SL Materials. The rebrand reflects its ambition to move beyond individual projects and build a wider European production footprint.
Circular construction moves toward scale
For investors, the deal highlights growing capital requirements around the circular economy. Construction is particularly exposed because it consumes large volumes of raw materials while generating significant waste.
That creates opportunities for technologies capable of recovering materials without sacrificing the performance required for new construction.
European policy is adding pressure. The region’s climate and circular economy objectives increasingly place resource efficiency alongside emissions reduction. That makes material recovery relevant not only to waste management, but also to corporate climate strategies and supply-chain resilience.
The challenge for companies such as SL Materials will be scale. Circular technologies must move beyond individual facilities and demonstrate that recovered materials can compete reliably on quality, availability and cost.
The $112 million investment is intended to accelerate that transition.
If SL Materials can expand its technology across multiple European markets, its model could help shift concrete recycling from lower-value waste treatment toward closed-loop material recovery. For construction companies, investors and policymakers, that distinction will become increasingly important as Europe seeks to reduce both industrial emissions and dependence on virgin resources.

articles.full_text:
Google, Constellation Sign 20 Year Deal to Add 890 MW of Nuclear Power
- Google and Constellation Energy signed a 20-year power purchase agreement to add 890 MW of new nuclear capacity to the PJM grid.
- Constellation plans more than $4.3 billion in investment across nuclear facilities in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with the first uprate expected by 2028.
- A separate 15-year agreement covers 2,700 MW of existing generation, while an expanded technology partnership will deploy Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise across energy operations.
Google and Constellation Energy are expanding their energy partnership with a 20-year agreement designed to bring 890 MW of new nuclear capacity onto the PJM Interconnection grid.
The additional output will come from upgrades to 11 Constellation-owned nuclear units in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The companies said the investment will increase thermal and electrical efficiency at existing facilities, adding firm generation without building a new nuclear plant.
The agreement comes as electricity demand rises across the United States, driven by data centers, artificial intelligence, manufacturing and industrial electrification. For PJM, which serves about 67 million people, the challenge is increasingly how to add dependable capacity quickly while limiting pressure on consumers.
Private capital backs new nuclear capacity
Constellation expects to invest more than $4.3 billion in the program. The projects are expected to sustain roughly 4,400 existing jobs and create about 7,200 construction jobs during the buildout.
The 890 MW expansion is comparable to the output of a large conventional nuclear reactor. Unlike greenfield development, however, nuclear uprates can add generation by improving turbines, steam generators, digital controls and other systems at operating plants.
The first uprate is expected to enter service by 2028.
“We’re committed to meeting our growth responsibly by actively investing in clean, reliable power that brings new capacity to our nation’s grids,” stated Amanda Peterson Corio, global head of energy and power at Google. “Our agreement with Constellation to fund nuclear reactor uprates will strengthen the PJM grid, which serves 67 million people, all while protecting energy affordability and supporting local union jobs.”
The projects also align with the federal Utility Power Reactor Incremental Scaling Effort or UPRISE, which encourages investment that increases electricity output from the existing US nuclear fleet.
Google secures long-term supply as power demand rises
Alongside the nuclear uprates, Google and Constellation entered a 15-year energy supply agreement covering another 2,700 MW of generation in PJM.
The structure provides longer-term revenue certainty for existing assets while keeping their electricity available to the broader market.
It also responds to PJM’s “Bring Your Own Power” approach, which seeks ways for large electricity consumers to support additional supply as their demand expands. Google has positioned the investment as a way to support its growth without transferring infrastructure costs to residential ratepayers.
RELATED ARTICLE: Google Backs Texas Electric Freight Route
Demand flexibility forms another part of the agreement. Google plans to incorporate load-shaping and demand-response capabilities that can reduce non-critical electricity consumption when the grid is under stress.
“Preserving and expanding the output of the existing nuclear fleet and developing new clean generation is critical to meeting our nation’s growing energy needs while keeping costs affordable for homes and businesses,” said Joe Dominguez, chairman, president and CEO of Constellation. “This long-term clean energy collaboration with Google can serve as a model for how technology companies and the energy industry can work together to responsibly develop the digital economy and invest in our nation’s energy infrastructure in a way that delivers grid-wide benefits for all, funded by private entities.”
AI moves deeper into grid operations
The companies are also expanding their technology relationship through a five-year agreement involving Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise.
Constellation plans to integrate AI workflows into site selection, power-flow modeling, permitting and interconnection planning. The companies expect those tools to reduce engineering timelines and accelerate new capacity.
AI will also support asset monitoring, outage management and construction planning. Google Cloud infrastructure will be used to strengthen cybersecurity around operational technology networks connected to critical energy systems.
Beyond the current agreements, Google and Constellation have established a framework to explore new clean generation, energy storage and demand-response projects across the United States, with near-term attention focused on PJM.
For energy executives and investors, the structure illustrates how large technology companies may increasingly finance the power infrastructure required for AI growth. Instead of relying solely on new generation projects, the deal places existing nuclear assets, efficiency upgrades and demand flexibility at the center of the capacity strategy.
